summary: To ask a yes/no question, put 吗 ma at the end of the statement: 你喝茶。→ 你喝茶吗？ Nothing moves. A second way repeats the verb with 不 in between (A-not-A): 你喝不喝茶？, 是不是, 要不要, and with 有: 有没有 — then without 吗. To offer a choice, join the options with 还是 ‘or’: 你喝茶还是咖啡？ (no 吗); 或者 ‘or’ is for statements. There is no all-purpose ‘yes’ or ‘no’: you answer with the verb (喝。/ 不喝。, 有。/ 没有。, 是。/ 不是。) or with 对 ‘right’, 当然 ‘of course’, 也许 ‘maybe’. To a negative question 对 agrees with the negative: 你不喝咖啡吗？— 对，我不喝。

blocks.caption: Three ways to ask

items.title: 还是 — or? (asking for a choice)
points: 你要米饭还是面包？ Rice or bread?

items.title: 或者 — or (stating)
points: 我早饭喝茶或者咖啡。 For breakfast I drink tea or coffee.
你要茶或者咖啡吗？ Would you like some tea or coffee?

blocks.title: Answering a negative question
blocks.text: 你不喝咖啡吗？ ‘Don’t you drink coffee?’ — 对，我不喝。 ‘Right, I don’t.’ / 不，我喝。 ‘No — I do.’ 对 and 是 agree with what was said; German contradicts a negative question with doch, Chinese with 不 + the verb.

blocks.title: Short replies of S09
blocks.text: 真的吗？ ‘Really?’ — 当然！ ‘Of course!’ — 也许。 ‘Maybe.’ — 我也是。 ‘Me too.’

blocks.title: Question words never take 吗
blocks.text: 你喝什么？ ‘What do you drink?’ — with 吗 (你喝什么吗？) it means ‘Do you drink anything?’.

blocks.title: A-not-A with two-syllable verbs
blocks.text: 喜欢 → 喜欢不喜欢 or the shorter 喜不喜欢 — both are heard: 你喜欢不喜欢鱼？

askYourself: Is there already a question word (什么, 哪里 …)? → no 吗.
Is it a yes/no question? → statement + 吗, or verb-不-verb.
Did I use verb-不-verb (要不要, 是不是)? → then no 吗.
Is the verb 有? → the A-not-A form is 有没有.
Do I offer a choice between two things? → A 还是 B, without 吗.
Is it a statement with ‘or’? → 或者.
How do I answer? → repeat the verb, or its negation (要 / 不要; 有 / 没有; 是 / 不是).
Was the question negative (你不 … 吗？)? → 对 confirms the negative: 对，我不喝.
steps: Write the statement in normal word order.
Add 吗 before the question mark — or replace the verb by verb + 不 + verb — or join two options with 还是.

traps: *你喝什么吗？ for ‘what do you drink?’ — 什么 + 吗 means ‘anything’.
*你要不要咖啡吗？ — A-not-A and 吗 never combine.
Don’t invert subject and verb as German does: 你喝茶吗？ keeps the statement order.
Answering 是 to every question sounds wrong: to 你要咖啡吗？ answer 要。, not 是。
*你喝茶或者咖啡？ to offer a choice → 你喝茶还是咖啡？
*你喝茶还是咖啡吗？ — a 还是 question takes no 吗.
To ‘Don’t you drink coffee?’ the answer 对 means ‘right, I don’t’.

notes.text: Greek asks yes/no questions by intonation alone (Πίνεις τσάι;); Chinese needs 吗 or verb-不-verb — raising the voice is not enough. ναι / όχι have no single Chinese match: answer with the verb (喝 / 不喝).
Russian asks by intonation (Ты пьёшь чай?) or with literary ли; Chinese adds 吗 at the end. да / нет become the verb: 喝 / 不喝, 有 / 没有.
Spanish asks by intonation (¿Bebes té?); Chinese adds 吗. sí / no become the verb: 喝 / 不喝.

English inverts or uses ‘do’ (Do you drink tea?); Chinese keeps the statement and adds 吗: 你喝茶吗？ There is no all-purpose yes / no: 喝 / 不喝, 是 / 不是. To a negative question 对 confirms the negative (‘right, I don’t’).
French est-ce que makes a question without changing the order — like 吗, but at the other end of the sentence. oui / non / si become the verb in Chinese.
German inverts (Trinkst du Tee?) and answers a negative question with doch; Chinese keeps the order, adds 吗, contradicts with 不 + verb or confirms with 对.
Hindi क्या at the start marks a yes/no question without changing the order (क्या तुम चाय पीते हो?) — like 吗, but at the beginning. हाँ / नहीं become the verb in Chinese.
Persian āyā at the start may mark a question without changing the order; Chinese 吗 at the end is the normal way. bale / na become the verb in Chinese.
Marathi का at the end of the sentence (तू चहा पितोस का? ‘do you drink tea?’) is exactly 吗.
Arabic hal at the start marks a yes/no question (hal tashrabu shāy?); Chinese puts 吗 at the end. naʿam / lā become the verb in Chinese.
Hebrew asks mostly by intonation (ata shote te?), formally with ha-im at the start; Chinese adds 吗 at the end. ken / lo become the verb in Chinese.

Turkish mı / mi / mu / mü is a question particle like 吗, but it follows the word asked about and changes its vowel; 吗 always closes the sentence and never changes. evet / hayır become the verb in Chinese.
Japanese か at the end of the sentence (お茶を飲みますか) is exactly 吗. Japanese はい to a negative question also confirms the negative — like Chinese 对.
Korean marks questions with the verb ending and intonation (차 마셔요?); Chinese adds the separate word 吗. Korean 네 to a negative question confirms the negative — like 对.
Finnish puts -ko / -kö on the first word and moves the verb first (Juotko teetä?); Chinese changes nothing and adds 吗. But Finnish answers by repeating the verb (Juon / En juo) — exactly like 喝 / 不喝.
Hungarian asks by intonation alone (Teát iszol?) or with -e; Chinese adds 吗. igen / nem become the verb in Chinese.
Swahili asks by intonation or with je at the start (Je, unakunywa chai?); Chinese adds 吗 at the end.
Luganda asks yes/no questions by intonation; Chinese needs 吗 or verb-不-verb, because the pitch of each syllable already belongs to its tone.
Vietnamese có … không? frames the verb (anh có uống trà không?) — the nearest relative of 有没有 and 喝不喝; Chinese also has the simpler 吗.
Inuktitut makes a question with a special verb ending (an interrogative mood); Chinese leaves the verb alone and adds 吗.

seeAlso.note: German puts the verb first (Trinkst du Tee?) and contradicts a negative question with doch; Chinese keeps the statement order, adds 吗, and answers with the verb.
Arabic opens the question with hal or ʾa-; Chinese closes it with 吗. Arabic أَمْ ‘or’ in questions vs أَوْ in statements is the same split as 还是 / 或者.
Hebrew often uses intonation alone (or הַאִם at the start); Chinese keeps its tones and uses 吗 instead.

quiz.why: Statement + 吗; A-not-A never takes 吗.
还是 asks for a choice, without 吗.
A-not-A is a plain yes/no question.

quiz.q: 你不吃肉吗？ — 对。 means …
quiz.why: 对 agrees with the negative question.

quiz.q: ‘For breakfast I drink tea or coffee.’
quiz.why: In a statement ‘or’ is 或者.
